source.title: Multiple Descent in the Multiple Random Feature Model
source.authors: Xuran Meng; Jian-Feng Yao; Yuan Cao

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether risk curves can have multiple descents in multi-component random-feature regression, a different model class and method from the deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own risk-curve results and experiments. The text says theoretical curves and empirical results match; values visible only in plots are recorded as figure only. Results cited from other studies, including claims about optimally tuned regularization, are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives asymptotic prediction risks and tests them in simulations of ridge regression with concatenated random features. Its own results test post-interpolation descent, multiple peaks, and dependence on regularization and SNR (V4 and V6).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors derive asymptotic excess-risk formulas, theoretically establish triple descent for suitable DRFMs, and demonstrate quadruple and quintuple descent in MRFMs. Component scale differences explain peak multiplicity, dimension ratios predict peak locations, and regularization and SNR affect risk curves. They do not establish elimination by optimally tuned regularization.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical and simulation study of ridge regression with concatenated random features, not a reproduction of the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak count, prominence, and location vary with activation-function scale and the ratio between feature dimensions. Regularization strength changes the curves. SNR affects risk trends in the under- and highly over-parameterized regimes.
record.problems: The empirical curves are presented in figures without stated error bars or confidence intervals. Simulations use the stated setup of 30 replications; the study does not test deep networks, epoch-wise descent, sample-wise descent, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peaks.

untested.parts: Model-wise double descent in deep networks; extending the findings to deep learning is future work.
Increasing training sample size near interpolation; the simulations fix n.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
Whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates peaks. Optimal regularization is discussed through prior literature; the study's own experiment sweeps fixed λ values.
Replotting risk against an effective parameter count and demonstrating an ordinary U-shaped curve.

missing.what: The theoretical triple-descent result: risk diverges at c=1 as λ→0 and at c=1+ψ2/ψ1 under sequential ridgeless and shrinking-second-feature limits, while intervening reference risks and the infinite-capacity limit are finite.
The bias contribution, as well as the noise-variance contribution, diverges at the two theoretical peak locations. With F1>0, the bias result permits peaks even when τ=0.
missing.locator: Appendix B.1, proofs of the second and fourth conclusions of Proposition 4.1; Equation (3.2)

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text describes figures but does not expose readable plotted values. Matched-SNR pairs having the same shape do not show invariance across different SNRs and do not justify the record's SNR limits_scope verdict. Appendix D's SNR definition and its displayed risk-scaling expression are internally inconsistent about squaring; preserve F1 and τ rather than infer numerical SNR values.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and model-wise test error in the specified deep-network setting.
Varying training sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests random-feature regression models, not all model classes.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Whether label noise or variance causes the peaks, and whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates them; the study varies SNR and regularization but does not establish either of those claims.
Recounting complexity by an effective number of parameters and testing whether that yields an ordinary U-shaped curve.
